candidates.title: Show HN: Universal Blindspot Detector (AI meta-analysis)
candidates.raw_content: This is a rough "blindspot detector" for AI conversations. Basically, the tool reframes conversations and tries to find the smallest moves the user COULD have made to have surfaced unknown assumptions for whatever problem they were solving. The goal is to show the value of using AI as a reflective surface to search for "unknown unknowns" or "things YOU didn't know you needed to know". ------------------------- The basic premise is this: For any given AI conversation, the quality of the output (for the specified goal) depends on the context from which decisions can be made. You can learn to surface assumptions (the AI's AND your own) and get better output from informed decisions. Best of all, when operating in this way, you have to actively engage the problem and strategy to accomplish this, so you don't lose understanding or creative agency. When you iterate during problem definition or strategy planning, it's cheaper and more efficient, too. For example: [# of Planning Phase Iterations] x 1,000 tokens [# of Strategy Phase Iterations] x 3,000 tokens [# of Execution Output Phase Iterations] x 5,000,000 tokens Usually when we are solving problems with this method, we one-shot the output even with local models like Qwen 3.6/3.8, spending FAR less time in the expensive execution phase. --------------------------- Anyway, please have a look! Totally free, no signup, you just need to export conversations in specific formats and upload them. This was made by myself and a few interns in a barn while doing indie game development ... and costs us money, so please don't abuse it. candidates.title: augmenting human intellect when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory. i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else. the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it. the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine. he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system. somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology. more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening. and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for. i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined. that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works? sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work. but not everything difficult is overhead. sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question. i want tools that leave room for that relationship. in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach. he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse. not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard. a system you can reshape as your understanding changes. this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself. the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller. but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment. i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us. i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before. what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission? when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean. not a world that no longer needs us. a world we have more ability to shape.

candidates.title: I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long. Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's. But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries: Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it. Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing. Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications. 📌 Watch my full Genie 4 tutorial to see how I created the worlds in the reel below: https://t.co/GvzPewT5gj

candidates.title: Vercel CI solves the "AI coding bottleneck" via: ① Fast and stable infrastructure (faster work) ② Turborepo integration (less work) ③ Agentic CI ① is obvious. Your CI is slow, flaky, goes down. We solve that. We operate 20 worldwide clusters doing millions of microVMs per day. ② is less obvious, but very powerful. Turborepo was designed to intelligently skip and cache prior work. The graph of dependencies is computed, not written. Ask your agent to migrate to @turborepo and start saving money and time. Even if you don't use us. But you should, it's really good. ③ is a game-changer. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚌𝚒 in the CLI is the first step, because now your agents can inspect, abort, trigger, replay CI. Vercel Agent can help optimize it. And this is just the start. You can expect a lot of hooks and capabilities to make CI something far more intelligent, that can even capture the nuance and judgment an engineer would have ("Are those tests even worth running?") Agentic CI is the future of how we ship software. Excited to build it with you all!

candidates.title: This is a LP letter that we recently wrote with our lessons on spotting talent from a decade of investing at the frontier. https://t.co/v1TnHjvAox The most common thing you hear about early stage investing is that "It is 90% about the founder".
